soil-chem-113.title: Redox: the electron trade behind rust and breath
soil-chem-113.text: A rusting nail and a breathing animal run the same kind of chemistry. Redox, short for reduction–oxidation, is any reaction in which the oxidation states of the reactants change. Oxidation is a loss of electrons, or a rise in oxidation state. Reduction is a gain of electrons, or a fall in oxidation state. The two always happen together. Neither can occur on its own. When iron rusts, the iron is oxidized to an oxide, while oxygen is reduced by taking up the electrons the iron releases. The same trade powers respiration, photosynthesis, combustion and the corrosion of metals. The words are older than the idea of the electron. Oxidation first meant reacting with oxygen. Reduction meant the weight lost when ore is heated to extract its metal. Both were later widened to mean electron transfer. The word redox itself first appeared in a 1928 article by Leonor Michaelis and Louis B. Flexner. In soils, sediments and water, redox differs from place to place. Those differences drive the cycling of elements through living things and their surroundings, as {{ref:soil-chem-121}} shows.

soil-chem-118.title: Electrons and protons, the two currencies of soil chemistry
soil-chem-118.text: Every chemical reaction in soil trades protons, electrons or some mix of the two. Redox in soils is the set of electron-transfer reactions beneath many soil processes and properties. Soil scientists track it as a voltage, Eh, explained in {{ref:soil-chem-123}}, or as pe, the negative log of electron activity, read much like pH. With pH, it is a master variable that both controls and reflects soil reactions. Early theory grew out of flooded soils and rice growing. It shaped later work on redox thermodynamics and the growth of plant roots, then spread to heavy metals, soil formation, organic compounds, mapping wet ground and cleanup. Microbes organize along electron transport chains, even building electrically conductive films and networks of bacterial nanowires. Redox also marks the soil itself, and its color features are critical clues for interpreting soils. Understanding how redox changes through a soil matters for carbon storage, cleanup by microbes, marking the edges of wet land and soil-based microbial fuel cells.

soil-chem-120.title: Rust spots and gray streaks: redox written in soil color
soil-chem-120.text: A soil's colors can record years of wetting and drying. Redoximorphic features are color patterns made when iron or manganese is oxidized, reduced and moved, so pigment is lost or gained against the soil's background color, its matrix. A matrix colored by ferrous iron, the reduced form, also counts. A pattern earns the name only once the processes behind it are known or inferred. Reducing conditions leave disrupted color: complex mottles and points of concentrated color. Aerobic conditions give uniform or gradual changes instead. As a wet soil dries and oxygen returns, reduced iron can re-oxidize locally into bright yellow-brown mottles. These features extend the story of {{ref:soil-found-028}} and give critical information for interpreting soils. The voltage measured in a soil, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-123}}, expresses how likely such reactions are. Classification relies on them too. Among the cracking clay soils of {{ref:soil-class-106}}, those with aquic conditions and these features form one named group, and the WRB suffix σ marks permanent saturation without them.

soil-chem-119.title: Breathing and photosynthesis as electron transfers
soil-chem-119.text: Every breath is a redox reaction. Aerobic respiration oxidizes fuels such as glucose and reduces oxygen to water. Photosynthesis does roughly the opposite: it reduces carbon dioxide to sugars and oxidizes water to oxygen. It complements respiration, yet it is not simply its reverse. Living things often store and release energy through such reactions, relying on the steady cycling of the carriers NAD+ and NADH.

soil-chem-114.title: Oxidizing agents, the electron takers
soil-chem-114.text: Of all electron acceptors, oxygen pulls hardest. An oxidizing agent oxidizes another substance by taking its electrons, and is itself reduced in the process. It is also called an oxidant or electron acceptor. Oxidants usually hold elements in high oxidation states, as permanganate does, or are highly electronegative elements such as oxygen and chlorine. In oxidizing soils, oxygen accepts electrons and is reduced to water.

soil-chem-115.title: Reducing agents, the electron givers
soil-chem-115.text: In soil, the main giver of electrons is soil organic matter. A reducing agent reduces another substance by giving it electrons, and is itself oxidized. It is also called a reductant or electron donor. Electropositive metals such as lithium, sodium, magnesium, iron, zinc and aluminium give up electrons readily, which makes them good reducing agents. Underground, donors include that same material, hydrogen, methane, reduced sulfur and iron compounds, and ammonium. Biochemists speak of a reducing equivalent: whatever transfers the equivalent of one electron, whether an electron or a hydrogen atom.

soil-chem-116.title: Redox couples: splitting a reaction into halves
soil-chem-116.text: The naming trips up many students. In any redox reaction the reductant passes electrons to the oxidant, so the reductant is oxidized and the oxidant reduced. That is why the reagent that gets oxidized is called the reducing agent. The two agents in a given reaction form a redox pair. A redox couple is a reducing species and its oxidized form, such as Fe2+ and Fe3+. The oxidation and the reduction, taken alone, are each a half-reaction. In electrochemical reactions the two halves happen at the same time but in different places.

soil-chem-117.title: Standard electrode potential: ranking the electron takers
soil-chem-117.text: Fluorine scores +2.866 V, zinc ions −0.763 V, and hydrogen ions exactly zero. These are standard electrode potentials: the equilibrium voltage of a half-reaction under standard conditions, measured against a standard hydrogen electrode. Also called a reduction potential, the value measures how strongly an oxidizing agent tends to be reduced. Hydrogen sits at zero by definition. Stronger oxidants score positive, weaker ones negative. The value is given in volts or millivolts. A cell's potential is the cathode potential minus the anode potential.

soil-chem-130.title: Biofilters: letting microbes eat the pollution
soil-chem-130.text: Engineers have hired microbes to clean water since 1893, when England introduced the trickling filter for wastewater. A biofilter is a bioreactor holding living material that captures pollutants and breaks them down biologically. Microorganisms attach to a bed of sand, crushed rock or gravel and grow into a thin living film that degrades the pollutants. Biofilters treat wastewater, catch harmful chemicals or silt washed off the land, and oxidize air pollutants. Bioswales, wetlands and riparian zones work the same way. One drawback: buildup of biomass can clog the bed.

soil-chem-123.title: Eh, the voltage that tells oxidizing soil from reducing soil
soil-chem-123.text: A cultivated field typically reads between +300 and +500 mV. Redox potential, written Eh, is the tendency of electrons to pass from an electron donor to an electron acceptor, measured in volts. It is zero for the standard hydrogen electrode couple, the reference from {{ref:soil-chem-117}}. Positive values mean an oxidizing setting that accepts electrons; negative values, a reducing one that donates them. It can be calculated from half-reactions with the Nernst equation. Three things set it: the oxidation state of the species present, pH and the amount of oxygen. Higher potentials occur at lower pH. Soil Eh generally spans −300 to +900 mV. Plants are generally held to tolerate +300 to +700 mV, and in the soils of wet land 300 mV divides aerobic from anaerobic conditions. Aerated waters usually read positive, while submerged soils, swamps and marine sediments normally read negative. Microbes sort by it. Strict aerobes are generally active at positive Eh and strict anaerobes at negative Eh. Facultative anaerobes also work at negative Eh when nitrate or sulfate is present.

soil-chem-131.title: Destroying pollution underground with strong oxidizers
soil-chem-131.text: In situ chemical oxidation injects strong oxidizers into contaminated soil or groundwater to destroy contaminants where they lie. Hydrogen peroxide was first used this way in 1985, on a formaldehyde spill in Springfield, Massachusetts. It treats many organic compounds, even some that resist natural breakdown, and suits chlorinated solvents and gasoline compounds such as benzene and toluene. Oxidants go in through rods or injection wells, or by soil mixing and hydraulic fracturing in tight ground. Success depends on the site's rocks, the dose, and real contact with the contaminant. Rising carbon dioxide signals that oxidation is working. Every main oxidant is hazardous to handle.

soil-chem-121.title: Redox gradients: oxidizing above, reducing below
soil-chem-121.text: The Earth as a whole is oxidizing at its surface and increasingly reducing below it. A redox gradient is a series of redox reactions sorted by redox potential. Such gradients form in space and in time, from differences in microbial processes, chemical makeup and oxidative potential. Oxygen supply, soil hydrology, the chemical species present and microbial activity drive them. They are typical of waterlogged soils, wetlands, lakes, coastal marshes, contaminant plumes and marine sediments. At large scale they are well understood. Redox at the micro-scale, in patchy, mixed settings, still needs more research and better ways to measure it.

soil-chem-122.title: The redox ladder: which electron acceptor goes first
soil-chem-122.text: Microbes spend their electron acceptors in a set order, best first. The redox ladder is that order, fixed by the free energy each redox pair yields. The most favorable reaction sits at the top, the least favorable at the bottom. From oxidizing to reducing, the usual sequence runs aerobic respiration, then nitrate reduction to nitrogen gas, then manganese, iron and sulfate reduction. For respiration without oxygen, the nitrate–nitrogen couple ranks just below oxygen, above manganese, iron, sulfate and, last of all, carbon dioxide to methane. In sediments, oxygen dwindles with depth, so these pathways stack in vertical layers. Yet thermodynamics alone does not decide where microbes live. Ecology and physiology matter too.

soil-chem-128.title: Breathing without oxygen: anaerobic respiration
soil-chem-128.text: A few millimetres of standing water are enough to smother a soil. Under that thin layer, bacteria that feed on soil organic matter use up the oxygen, forcing a switch to anaerobic respiration. This is respiration that ends its electron transport chain with an inorganic acceptor other than oxygen, such as nitrate, sulfate or sulfur. These acceptors have lower reduction potentials than oxygen, so less energy is released and the process is less efficient. It differs from fermentation, which passes electrons to organic compounds. Even well-aired soil holds oxygen-free pockets, because oxygen gas diffuses slowly. The products leave their mark. Nitrate respiration is the main route returning fixed nitrogen to the air as N2. Sulfate respiration makes hydrogen sulfide, the rotten-egg smell of coastal marshes. Aerobic respiration releases carbon dioxide, while anaerobic pathways such as {{ref:soil-chem-129}} release methane. Others change the oxidation state of iron and manganese. Bacterial sulfate reduction was discovered by the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-016}}. Because decay in waterlogged soils runs without oxygen, those soils store large amounts of organic carbon.

soil-chem-125.title: How a flooded soil runs out of oxygen
soil-chem-125.text: Flood a soil warmer than about 5 °C, and its microbes strip out the oxygen within a few days. Reduction in waterlogged soils is that shift from oxidizing to reducing conditions as oxygen runs out and anaerobic microbes take over. The fuel is soil organic matter, the main source of electrons in soil. Decomposers consume oxygen as they break it down, and Eh falls. Next, nitrate and ferric oxide are reduced. Iron tells the story. At high redox potential it is deposited as ferric hematite, the oxidized form. Under low redox conditions ferrous iron builds up, and decay slows. Prolonged saturation can dissolve ferric iron minerals that hold phosphorus, releasing it to leaching. Hydrology rules the process. Flooding turns soil from oxic to anoxic, and draining and drying restore its starting Eh. Even soil that is not saturated can hold small anoxic hotspots inside its pores.

soil-chem-129.title: Methanogenesis: the last step of decay without air
soil-chem-129.text: Methane has 25 times the global warming potential of carbon dioxide, averaged over 100 years, and wet soils make a lot of it. Methanogenesis is the making of methane by microbes called methanogens, all of them archaea, as the final step in breaking down dead plant and animal material without oxygen. It sits at the bottom of {{ref:soil-chem-122}}. Once every electron acceptor except carbon dioxide is spent, only methanogenesis and fermentation can proceed. Without it, much carbon would pile up as fermentation products. In most freshwater wetlands sulfate is scarce, and methanogenesis takes over only once sulfate is used up. In sediments, sulfate reducers take most of the hydrogen in upper layers, while methanogens dominate lower down. In the oxygen-free layers of {{ref:soil-class-070}}, they combine carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas into methane and water. Production runs high in flooded rice fields, wetlands, and anoxic floodplain, lake and reservoir sediments. Other microbes, methanotrophs, oxidize methane back to carbon dioxide. Aerating such soils raises sulfate and nitrate, which cut methane output. In upland soils, methanogenesis is often confined to anoxic microsites inside otherwise aerobic soil.

soil-chem-133.title: Paddy fields: rice, flooding and methane
soil-chem-133.text: Rice paddies release an estimated 50 to 100 million tonnes of methane a year, about 10% of global methane emissions. A paddy field is a flooded crop field used to grow semiaquatic crops, above all rice and taro. Paddy farming began in the Neolithic rice cultures of the Yangtze River basin and remains the dominant way to grow rice. Draining paddies so the soil aerates interrupts methane production and can boost yield. Ammonium-based fertilizers raise emissions. Early soil redox theory grew out of flooded paddy soils, and long wet-field cultivation can turn them into the human-made soils described in {{ref:soil-class-120}}.

soil-chem-132.title: Permanganate, Fenton's reagent, persulfate and ozone
soil-chem-132.text: Four strong oxidizers are the usual choices in {{ref:soil-chem-131}}: permanganate, Fenton's reagent, persulfate and ozone. Fenton's reagent, hydrogen peroxide catalysed by iron, and permanganate have the longest record. Permanganate needs double bonds in its targets and is used up by other carbon-based material in soil. Persulfate, introduced in the late 1990s, avoids both problems. Fenton's reagent makes hydroxyl radicals but needs lowered pH to keep iron dissolved. Whether field use at near-neutral pH is truly a Fenton reaction remains disputed. Ozone, about 12 times more soluble than oxygen, is injected from below so its bubbles rise through the contamination.

soil-chem-124.title: Measuring Eh with a platinum electrode
soil-chem-124.text: Soil Eh is read with a platinum electrode, referenced to the standard hydrogen electrode. Measuring redox potential means either sampling in the field for lab analysis or placing an electrode in soil or water for readings on the spot. Each choice has a cost. Many samples give fine detail across space but little over time. Fixed electrodes give continuous readings but cover little ground. Waters, soils and sediments can be highly patchy, which complicates both. Induced-polarization imaging can track redox finely in space and time, though its signal is not yet fully understood.

soil-chem-126.title: Microbes that sharpen the gradients they live on
soil-chem-126.text: Microbes do more than live along redox gradients: they sharpen them. By switching how they respire, to sulfate reduction or methanogenesis for instance, they suit local conditions and amplify the gradient. Organic pollutants break down fastest where oxygenated and oxygen-free zones meet, such as the groundwater capillary fringe, because electron donors and acceptors abound there. Cable bacteria, which oxidize sulfide, link zones short of electrons with zones holding a surplus. Thin films of metal- or sulfate-reducing bacteria create gradients on the micrometre scale.

soil-chem-127.title: Redox layers in lakes, seas and their sediments
soil-chem-127.text: Water columns and the mud beneath them carry redox gradients of their own. Oxic, suboxic and hypoxic water layers, from well oxygenated to poorly oxygenated, each allow different redox reactions. Oxygen minimum zones add to the layering. In bottom sediments, gradients arise from differences in minerals, dead organic material, structure and sorption. Slow electron transport and varied pore sizes make these sediments highly patchy.

openers.redox-and-soil-chemistry: Rust on iron and breath in the lungs share one chemistry: redox, short for reduction–oxidation, in which electrons pass from one substance to another. A donor gives electrons, an acceptor takes them, and each half of that trade has a voltage that can be measured. In soil, these transfers underlie many processes and properties, from the respiration of microbes to the gray and rust-colored patterns left by iron and manganese. This chapter follows them from single reactions to the electrical tendency of a whole soil and the ordered series of reactions it supports. It ends with the ways people use oxidation and microbes to clean polluted ground and water.

reviews.redox-and-soil-chemistry: Redox comes down to a trade: a reducing agent gives electrons, an oxidizing agent takes them, and each half of the trade has a voltage. Measured in soil as Eh, that tendency sorts reactions into gradients and a ladder, with oxygen at the top and methane-making at the bottom. When water fills the pores, microbes burn through oxygen, then nitrate, iron and sulfate, until a wetland or paddy field releases methane. The iron left behind, as a gray matrix or yellow-brown mottles, records those swings in the soil's own color. People turn the same chemistry to use, with biofilters that let microbes break down pollutants and strong oxidizers injected to destroy contaminants underground.
